Coal
kōl
n. (a burning ember; rendering Hebrew gachelet, retseph, Greek anthrax)
From Anglo-Saxon col. In Scripture a coal is almost always live — a burning ember taken from an altar or a hearth, never inert fuel.

Biblical Definition

Coal in the Authorized Version means a live ember, and it is nearly always taken from a fire that is already burning to God. On the Day of Atonement the high priest takes “a censer full of burning coals of fire from off the altar before the LORD” and carries them within the vail (Lev 16:12) — the incense of intercession must be kindled by altar fire, not by any fire of a man's own. Isaiah's cleansing follows the same rule: a seraph takes a live coal from the altar and touches his unclean lips. The Psalter uses coals for theophany — “coals were kindled by it” (Psa 18:8), “hail stones and coals of fire” (Psa 18:12) — and Elijah, at the end of himself under the juniper, is fed a cake baken on the coals (1Ki 19:6): the same element that pictures wrath also bakes bread for an exhausted prophet. Paul then makes coals an instrument of love: “thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head” by feeding an enemy (Rom 12:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines coal as a piece of wood or other combustible substance ignited and burning, or charred and extinguished — noting the Scriptural use of live coals from the altar.

expand to see more

COAL, n. A piece of wood, or other combustible substance, ignited, burning, or charred.

2. In the plural, coals, embers; live coals.

3. A solid, opake, inflammable substance found in the earth, and dug from mines.

To heap coals of fire on the head, to excite by kindness the pangs of remorse in an enemy.

Key Scripture

Lev 16:12 — "And he shall take a censer full of burning coals of fire from off the altar before the LORD, and his hands full of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the vail:"

Psa 18:12 — "At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hail stones and coals of fire."

1Ki 19:6 — "And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again."

Rom 12:20 — "Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head."

Modern Corruption

Strange fire — worship kindled from a source God did not appoint — presented as zeal, while Romans 12:20 is read as a permission to wound rather than a command to feed.

expand to see more

Leviticus 16:12 specifies where the coals come from: off the altar before the LORD. Nadab and Abihu died for offering incense with fire God had not commanded, and the principle governs worship still. Zeal, sincerity, and heat are not sufficient; the fire must be taken from the altar of atonement, which is to say that acceptable worship is kindled by the finished sacrifice and by nothing else. Every innovation that generates its own heat — emotional, aesthetic, or theatrical — is offering strange fire, however sincerely.

Romans 12:20 is often quoted with a smirk, as though heaping coals meant a superior form of revenge. Read the command it is attached to: if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink. The coals are the burning of shame that leads to repentance, and the instrument is a meal. Webster's definition catches it exactly — to excite by kindness the pangs of remorse. A Christian who uses the verse to justify hostility has inverted the only sentence it appears in.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gachelet (H1513), a live coal, burning ember; ritspah (H7531), a hot stone or coal — the seraph's coal in Isa 6:6; Greek anthrax (G440), a burning coal.

expand to see more

Hebrew gachelet (H1513) — a live coal; the censer of coals from the altar on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:12).

Hebrew ritspah (H7531) — a live coal or hot stone; taken with tongs from the altar to touch Isaiah's lips (Isa 6:6).

Greek anthrax (G440) — a burning coal; Paul's coals of fire heaped by feeding an enemy (Rom 12:20).

Usage

"“A censer full of burning coals of fire from off the altar” — incense kindled by altar fire only."

"“A cake baken on the coals” — the same element bakes bread for a spent prophet."

"“Thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head” — and the instrument is a meal."
